findings.problem: The section tells the candidate that reading 'Schedule VI' as 'a sixth and gentlest tier of controlled-substance regulation' is a misreading, because 'in substance it is the set of ordinary prescription medicines'. Under Massachusetts law that reading is correct: every Schedule VI drug is a Massachusetts controlled substance. The section never says so. And ma_vs_federal[0] leaves out the distinction the declared subtopic most needs: Schedule VI drugs are controlled substances under Massachusetts law, but they are not federally controlled.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, § 1 defines 'controlled substance' as a drug, substance, controlled substance analogue or immediate precursor 'in any schedule or class referred to in this chapter'. § 3(6) makes Schedule VI a statutory schedule: a prescription drug not included in Schedules I through V. § 2(a) directs the Commissioner to establish the sixth schedule as part of regulating the manufacture, distribution, dispensing and possession of controlled substances. The regulation says the same. 105 CMR 700.002 opens 'The following schedules of controlled substances are established' before subsections (A) through (F). 105 CMR 700.001 defines 'Controlled Substance' in the same terms, and defines 'Additional Drug' as 'a controlled substance in Schedule VI'. 105 CMR 700.006(I)(3) sets 'controlled substances listed in Schedule VI' against 'non-controlled substances'. Massachusetts consequences attach through that status. For example, c. 94C, § 7(a) requires registration of non-pharmacy persons who dispense 'any controlled substance', and 105 CMR 700.006(F)(4) requires records of Schedule VI sample medications. The accurate teaching is that Schedule VI is Massachusetts's least restrictive controlled-substance schedule. It carries no federal controls and none of the Massachusetts Schedule II-V rules, but it is not outside controlled-substance regulation. A candidate following the section would mark false a true proposition: in Massachusetts, a prescription drug outside Schedules I-V is a controlled substance.

findings.problem: The scenario asks whether a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug carries 'the record and reporting duties that attach to controlled substances'. The resolution answers that 'nothing else follows automatically', and it labels 'reading Schedule VI as a sixth tier of controlled-substance regulation' part of the error. That gives a Massachusetts candidate the wrong frame. The drug is a Massachusetts controlled substance in Schedule VI, and some Massachusetts record and reporting rules do reach Schedule VI.
findings.rationale: The authorities are the same as for the orientation[2] finding. In addition, three rules reach Schedule VI. 105 CMR 700.006(I)(3) requires pharmacies in registered health facilities to file prescriptions for 'controlled substances listed in Schedule VI' in a designated file. 105 CMR 700.006(F)(4) requires a registered practitioner to keep records of Schedule VI sample medications dispensed. 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) makes a Schedule VI drug MassPAT-reportable when the Department classifies it as an additional drug. The correct resolution has three parts. No federal controlled-substance duty arises, because the drug is not in 21 CFR 1308.11-1308.15. No Massachusetts Schedule II-V duty arises either. But the drug is a Massachusetts Schedule VI controlled substance, so the candidate must open the Massachusetts rule for the act, which may or may not impose a duty. The error the scenario invites is importing federal and Schedule II-V duties. Recognising Schedule VI as a controlled-substance schedule is not an error.

findings.problem: The section says five times that Schedule VI status does not by itself make a drug routinely MassPAT-reportable, but it never says what does. The key to retrieval_prompts[4] ('False') is right, but neither of the two reasons it gives explains why a MassPAT-reportable drug need not be federally scheduled. The real reason is the additional-drug category, which the section never mentions. A candidate can therefore come away believing that Schedule VI drugs are never reportable.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, § 24A(a)(1) directs monitoring of 'all schedule II to V, inclusive, controlled substances and certain additional drugs'. It defines additional drugs as substances the Department determines to carry a bona fide potential for abuse. 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) applies the pharmacy reporting duty to dispensing of Schedule II-V controlled substances and of 'a controlled substance classified by the Department as an additional drug'. 105 CMR 700.001 defines 'Additional Drug' as 'a controlled substance in Schedule VI determined by the Department to carry a bona fide potential for abuse'. So a Schedule VI drug the Department has designated is reportable even though it is not federally scheduled. Option B of the attached practice question turns on exactly this. The section names the MassPAT framework without conveying its content.

findings.problem: MA-Q-0009 (select all that apply; key A, B, C, D) cannot be answered from the section. The section supports rejecting E, because a Schedule VI classification imports no federal Schedule III-IV refill rule. It also supports the first half of B, because a prescription drug absent from 21 CFR 1308.11-1308.15 is Massachusetts Schedule VI. But it gives no basis for selecting A, C or D, or for the reportability half of B. Its drug_examples field is empty, and it states neither the Schedule II refill bar, nor the MassPAT scope, nor the CMEA retail controls.
findings.rationale: Pregabalin is listed in 21 CFR 1308.15(e). It is therefore Schedule V under both federal and Massachusetts law (via 105 CMR 700.002(E)), and Schedule V dispensing is reportable under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1). Gabapentin appears in none of 21 CFR 1308.11-1308.15, so whether it is reportable depends on the additional-drug designation (see the retrieval_prompts[4] finding). Methylphenidate is listed in 21 CFR 1308.12(d), and 21 CFR 1306.12(a) prohibits refilling a Schedule II prescription. Pseudoephedrine appears in none of 1308.11-1308.15, and its retail controls come from a separate regime the section does not cover. The section does not contradict the key, but it pulls a candidate away from two correct options. Its unrelieved negative framing of MassPAT works against B. Its insistence that the schedule 'does not itself answer' refill questions works against C, although 1306.12(a) attaches the refill prohibition directly to the Schedule II listing. Either map MA-Q-0009 to the sections that teach those rules, or add the missing content here.

findings.problem: Two statements accurately describe 105 CMR 700.002(A)-(E) as currently written: 'Massachusetts does not maintain a rival list', and 'for Schedules I through V there is no separate Massachusetts scheduling decision to look up'. As statements of Massachusetts law, though, they are too categorical. The statute provides mechanisms, beyond Schedule VI, by which the Massachusetts and federal classifications of a substance can diverge.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 700.002(A)-(E) do incorporate 21 CFR 1308.11-1308.15 by reference, and 700.002 contains no Massachusetts-specific entries. The statute, however, allows Massachusetts to act on its own. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 2(a½) lets the Commissioner delete or reschedule substances by regulation, and requires a corresponding Massachusetts regulation within 30 days of new or up-scheduled federal control. § 2A lets the Commissioner place a substance that is not otherwise scheduled in Schedule I temporarily, by order. The order is an emergency regulation and can remain in effect for up to one year. § 3 permits scheduling on Massachusetts findings. The statement should be qualified to the current regulation, and should note that a Massachusetts order or regulation can place or move a substance independently.

findings.problem: Two statements overstate the point: 'Membership is therefore a matter of appearing on a list under some name, not of belonging to a pharmacologic family', and 'the schedules list substances by name'. The Schedule II paragraph the section itself relies on reaches a category defined by statute, not only named substances.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1308.12(b)(1) covers 'opium and opiate, and any salt, compound, derivative, or preparation of opium or opiate'. Under 21 CFR 1300.01(a), a term Part 1300 leaves undefined takes its meaning from 21 U.S.C. 802. 21 U.S.C. 802(18) defines 'opiate' or 'opioid' as a substance with addiction-forming or addiction-sustaining liability similar to morphine. So membership can turn on a defined property as well as on a name. Worked example 3 still reaches the right conclusion: receptor activity is not the test, and the named exclusions and placements elsewhere control. But the rule it teaches should tell candidates to read the defined terms and the class-wide listings, not only the names.

results.summary: The federal content is accurate against current eCFR (data through 2026-09-09). I verified the Part 1308 architecture and the opening formula shared by 1308.11-1308.15. The code-number sentence appears in 1308.11-1308.14 only, which matches the section's word 'most'. I also verified the 'unless specifically excepted or unless listed in another schedule' prefaces, 1308.12(b)(1)(i), every exclusion worked example 3 names, 1308.13(e)(1)(ii), 1308.14(b)(1), and 1308.15(c)(1) and (c)(6). 1308.15(c) carries no such preface, so worked example 2 resolves its overlap correctly. The section quotes and characterises 105 CMR 700.002(A)-(F) correctly. The serious defect is on the Massachusetts side. The section teaches that treating Schedule VI as a tier of controlled-substance regulation is a misreading. In fact M.G.L. c. 94C, §§ 1, 2(a) and 3(6) and 105 CMR 700.001-700.002 make every Schedule VI drug a Massachusetts controlled substance (High, restated at worked_examples[0].resolution). The section also invokes MassPAT repeatedly without stating the Schedule VI additional-drug rule (Medium). Its only practice question, MA-Q-0009, cannot be answered from it (Medium). Four Low findings concern statements that are overbroad or incomplete. Targeted edits fix all of these without restructuring the section. It is not publishable as it stands: MINOR_EDIT.
